reader.title: Shooting of Lazard James
bases: A deputy sheriff, on tax-collection duty, shot Lazard James during an encounter at James's home; no crowd or mob was involved (A1).
Only one report, the local St. Landry Clarion, describes the shooting, and it gives the deputy's account (A1).

summary.text: The shooting of Lazard James took place in the Plaquemine Point section of St. Landry Parish, Louisiana, in late July 1903, when Deputy Sheriff Robert Milsted shot James, a Black landowner, through the eye during a dispute at James's home.
James was badly wounded but was expected to recover.
The only known account, in the Opelousas St. Landry Clarion, gave the deputy's version and presented the case as evidence of rising defiance among Black residents of the parish.
Milsted served as collector of delinquent road taxes, and the Clarion described James as 30 years old and the owner of "a good place."
According to the paper, the deputy went to James's house on the Friday before its 25 July issue about a cow and noticed that James's buggy lacked the required road-tax tag.
In the Clarion's telling, James answered "saucily" that the tag was none of the deputy's business, and Milsted went back to the barn to check the buggy again.
On his return he found James in a lane near the house cursing the sheriff and his deputies.
The paper said James seized Milsted around the waist and declared he would cut his throat, and that Milsted drew his pistol and fired "without aiming."
The shot made Milsted's horse buck and throw him, and the paper said James then got on top of him and tried to draw a knife.
Two passers-by separated the men, and only then was it found that James had been shot through the eye.
When Milsted got up and saw James's brother approaching with a shotgun, he left the neighborhood.
The Clarion reported that James was "badly shot" but was believed likely to recover.
No report of an arrest, a charge against either man, or James's later condition appears in the coverage.

The St. Landry Clarion ran the story on its front page on 25 July 1903 under the headline "Bad Nigger Attempfs to Kill Deputy-Sheriff Milsted," calling James "a bad nigger" and "a terror" among both whites and Blacks.
The article opened by blaming President Theodore Roosevelt for having "aroused the local bad niggers," and it tied the shooting to a recent case in which a Black man had whipped a white boy.
Its account came entirely from the officer's side; neither James nor his family was quoted.
No other white newspaper and no Black newspaper is known to have reported the shooting.

accounts.label: Deputy's account as told by the local paper
accounts.gist: James answered 'saucily' about a missing road-tax tag, then seized Milsted, threatened to cut his throat and tried to draw a knife; Milsted fired 'without aiming' and struggled with him until passers-by intervened.

framing.detail: The St. Landry Clarion headlined 'Bad Nigger Attempfs to Kill Deputy-Sheriff Milsted', called James 'a bad nigger' and 'a terror', and blamed President Roosevelt for arousing 'the local bad niggers'.
